Voyager Interstellar Mission — current position dashboard

Cape Canaveral, 1977-08-20. Launched 16 days BEFORE its twin Voyager 1, but on a slower trajectory that threads all four outer planets. The Grand Tour was the actual purpose — only Voyager 2's geometry could reach Uranus and Neptune via successive gravity assists. The alignment that made it possible was identified by Gary Flandro at JPL in 1965 and won't recur for ~175 years.

Closest approach 721,670 km on 1979-07-09. Discovers Europa's smooth water-ice surface and the first detailed images of Ganymede's bright/dark terrain; confirms Voyager 1's volcanic Io observations. Jupiter's gravity bends the trajectory outward toward Saturn 26 months later, the first of three planetary assists this mission will make.

Closest approach 101,000 km on 1981-08-26. Returns the most detailed Saturn-ring imagery to date (spokes, braided F-ring) and reveals the gross structure of Hyperion's chaotic tumble. The encounter geometry was constrained to thread the parking gate between Uranus and the deep south of the ecliptic — the only path that keeps both ice giants reachable.

Closest approach 81,500 km on 1986-01-24 — the only spacecraft visit to Uranus to date. Reveals the planet's extreme 98° axial tilt, 10 new moons, and a tilted magnetic field. Voyager 2's geometry takes it through the ring plane at 14.5 km/s; the slingshot then has to bend the trajectory ~50° to reach Neptune three years later.

Closest approach 4,950 km above Neptune's cloud tops on 1989-08-25 — closer than any other Voyager planet pass and the only spacecraft visit to Neptune ever. Five hours later flies past Triton at 40,000 km, imaging active nitrogen geysers on the moon's nitrogen-ice surface. With no remaining planetary target, the geometry bends the trajectory ~48° below the ecliptic; Voyager 2 crossed the heliopause on 2018-11-05.
Only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune; Grand Tour of four giant planets

Voyager 2 flew the tour that may never be flown again. Launched sixteen days before its twin on a slower, longer arc, it is the only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune — two worlds that remain, decades later, known to us almost entirely from the few hours it spent racing past each one. It found a planet tipped on its side, the fastest winds in the solar system, and a frozen moon venting geysers into space, and then it too crossed into interstellar space, in 2018. Every serious plan to return to the ice giants still rests on what this single spacecraft saw on its way out.

The twin that kept going when budgets tightened, Voyager 2 carried the Grand Tour from Jupiter and Saturn out to Uranus and Neptune — still the only close-up images we have of the ice giants. Its Neptune encounter in 1989 revealed the Great Dark Spot and Triton's geysers. Today both Voyagers sail in interstellar space with a golden record as humanity's calling card. Orrery lists Neptune as the catalogue destination; the real path relied on multiple gravity assists.
